passage: Lights-out in the girls' hostel was at ten, but at nine-forty Vasudha was still cross-legged on her bed, a small brass diya unlit in her hand. Her roommate Damini looked up from her notes. 'You've stopped lighting it.' 'I'm not sure what I'm doing when I light it,' Vasudha said. 'At home Amma does it and I just copied.' For weeks she had been borrowing library books, one on the Gita, one on Buddhist ideas, one by a scientist who believed in no god at all, and arguing with all of them in the margins of her notebook. 'So what do you believe?' Damini asked, not unkindly. Vasudha turned the diya over. 'That I want five quiet minutes every morning. The words, I'm still choosing.' She set the diya back on the shelf, facing the window.

qa.q: What time was lights-out in the hostel?
qa.a: Lights-out was at ten.

qa.q: Why had Vasudha stopped lighting the diya?
qa.a: She was unsure what it meant to her, since she had only copied Amma, and she wanted her practice to be her own choice.

qa.q: How could a warden or teacher support Vasudha's exploring?
qa.a: They could keep different books and views available and let her talk it through without pushing her toward any answer.

qa.q: How does Damini seem to see Vasudha's questioning?
qa.a: She notices the change and asks directly but kindly, which suggests curiosity rather than judgement.

grounding: Shows a teenager comparing belief systems and beginning to commit to a practice in her own terms.

passage:
Dear Kiran Didi,
Remember how you said you only worked out your own views in college? I think mine started this month. Papa took me to two ward meetings before the election. I went ready to agree with whoever he agreed with. But the first candidate talked about the lake near our school, and I actually cared, and the second talked about night buses for women who work late shifts, and I cared about that too. Papa likes only one of them. At dinner I said so, and it went quiet for a bit. He didn't get angry. He just said, 'Then read both manifestos properly.' So I am, with a pencil. I can't vote for two more years, but I want to know why I'd pick someone, not just who.
Love, Vasudha

qa.q: How many ward meetings did Papa take Vasudha to?
qa.a: He took her to two ward meetings.

qa.q: What does Vasudha's wish to know 'why' suggest about what she wants?
qa.a: She feels determined to make her political views her own reasoned choice rather than borrowed from Papa.

qa.q: What could Kiran write back that would help?
qa.a: She could share how she worked out her own views and encourage Vasudha to keep reading and questioning, wherever she lands.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Vasudha disagreed at dinner?
qa.a: He may have been surprised, since it went quiet, but his reply suggests he respects her thinking for herself. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teenager starting to form her own political views instead of taking on her father's.

passage: A year ago I was sure I'd be an architect, because everyone said I draw well. Then my aunt Jaya, who runs a small bakery in Kochi, let me help during the Christmas rush. "Elizabeth, you're on orders," she said. I didn't draw anything for two weeks. I counted orders, calmed an angry customer, and fixed the delivery list when two boys didn't turn up. By the end I noticed I was happiest not with the icing but when the chaos ran smoothly. So I made a list in two columns: what I'm good at, and what different jobs actually need. Drawing was there, but so were planning and talking to strangers. Now I'm looking at hotel management and event planning too. I haven't decided. But I've stopped picking a future just because it matched one compliment.

qa.q: Where is Aunt Jaya's bakery?
qa.a: It is in Kochi.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth notice about when she felt happiest?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt happiest when the busy rush ran smoothly, which was a surprise, since drawing had seemed to be the thing.

qa.q: How could a school counsellor support Elizabeth now?
qa.a: A counsellor could help Elizabeth explore a few fields that match the list and set up talks or short visits with people in those jobs.

qa.q: How might Aunt Jaya have seen Elizabeth during the rush?
qa.a: Aunt Jaya probably saw a dependable helper who handled problems calmly, and may have been glad to give her that experience.

grounding: Shows a teenager testing an assumed career against real experience and a list of her strengths.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 10 career week. Devika came to my table twice. The first time she said, 'My parents want engineering, and I'm fine at maths, so.' She didn't look at me. The second time, after the session with the wildlife researcher, she came back with her friend Dilnaz and a page of questions: which subjects, how much fieldwork, whether the pay is steady. She rated herself honestly: strong in biology, patient, 'bad with heat, but I could get used to it.' Dilnaz pointed out that Devika spends every Sunday at the bird sanctuary with her grandfather. Devika laughed but didn't deny it. Next step: I have given her two books on careers in ecology and suggested she discuss both paths at home with her question sheet in hand.

qa.q: What did Devika say the first time she came to the table?
qa.a: That her parents want engineering and she is fine at maths.

qa.q: What does Devika not looking at the counsellor the first time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was unsure or unexcited about the choice she was repeating.

qa.q: Why is suggesting she take the question sheet home a helpful step?
qa.a: It lets her talk with her parents using concrete facts about both paths, instead of arguing from feelings alone.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz seem to see Devika's interests?
qa.a: Dilnaz sees her friend's love of birds clearly and nudges her to take it seriously as a possible career.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager weighing her own strengths and interests against possible careers during career week.

passage: Tuesday night. Something small happened today but I can't stop thinking. At lunch the girls were laughing about Dilnaz's new haircut and I laughed too, and even added a joke. Then Dilnaz walked in and sat next to me like normal, and I felt sick. She has been my friend since Class 3. When Ammi was in hospital last year, Dilnaz came every evening with my notes. And I sold her out for one laugh. I don't want to be like that. I want to be the one who says 'leave it' even if it's awkward. Tomorrow I'll tell her, maybe not everything, but that I was mean and I'm sorry. And next time I'll actually say 'leave it' out loud. – Parveen

qa.q: Since which class has Dilnaz been Parveen's friend?
qa.a: Since Class 3.

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel sick when Dilnaz sat next to her?
qa.a: Parveen felt guilty for having just joked about a friend who had always been loyal.

qa.q: What would you advise Parveen for tomorrow?
qa.a: Apologise simply and honestly, then show the change by speaking up the next time the group mocks someone.

qa.q: If you were Dilnaz, what would you want from Parveen?
qa.a: I would want an honest apology and to know Parveen will stand by me when I'm not in the room. 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend she wants to be after letting a loyal friend down.

passage:
Hansa: i yelled at chotu again today. he just wanted me to see his drawing
Mahima: u were studying na?
Hansa: yes but i didn't even look up. he walked off so quietly 😔
Mahima: ugh that quiet walk away is the worst
Hansa: i keep saying i want to be the didi YOU were to me
Hansa: you always had 5 min for me even in your boards year
Mahima: haha i also yelled plenty, trust me
Mahima: but ya, 5 min is doable
Hansa: ok new rule. when he comes, pen down for 5 min. timer if needed
Mahima: and say sorry for today
Hansa: already did. he showed me the drawing. it's a dinosaur with my face 😅
Mahima: perfect. frame it ❤️

qa.q: What did Hansa's little brother want her to do?
qa.a: He wanted her to see his drawing.

qa.q: What does Hansa's sad emoji after 'he walked off so quietly' reveal?
qa.a: It shows she felt guilty and hurt seeing how quietly he gave up on her.

qa.q: What makes Hansa's new rule a good step?
qa.a: It is small and concrete, five minutes with the pen down, so she can keep it even while studying.

qa.q: How might Hansa's little brother experience the change?
qa.a: He would feel noticed and important when she stops for him, instead of learning not to ask.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager choosing what kind of older sister she wants to be, modelled on her cousin.

passage: Coach's note, inter-house practice, week three. Class 9 has split into two lunch groups, and it shows on the field: the 'front-row' group passes only to each other. Today Noor, who sits with that group, was put on a team with Manoj and two others from the other side. For ten minutes she hung back. Then Manoj saw her open and passed; she scored and he whooped. Afterwards I saw her glance toward her usual friends before walking off with her new teammates for water. One of her friends said something to her and she shrugged, face tight. Next step: I will mix teams by drawing lots every week, so no one has to cross over alone, and I'll keep an eye on how Noor is doing at lunch.

qa.q: How will teams be picked from next week?
qa.a: By drawing lots every week.

qa.q: What does Noor's glance toward her usual friends suggest she was worried about?
qa.a: She may have worried her friends would see walking off with the new teammates as leaving their group.

qa.q: Why might drawing lots help?
qa.a: It takes the choice out of students' hands, so mixing is not seen as betraying anyone's group.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen Noor after the goal?
qa.a: His whoop suggests he was glad to include her and saw her as a real teammate.

grounding: Shows how rigid group lines at school affect a teenager who crosses them, noticed by a coach.

passage: Friday. So Pema has been at school three weeks and still eats alone. He's actually funny; I found out in the chemistry lab when he gave all our test tubes names. Today I asked the guys if he could sit with us, and it went weird. Nobody said no. They just said 'he's not really our type' and changed the topic. What is our type? We're five boys who play the same game and wear the same shoes. I didn't push it. I hate that I didn't. Maybe on Monday I'll just go sit at his table instead. They can't kick me out of a table I leave. Or they can make it awkward forever. I'll decide on Monday. – Dhruv

qa.q: How long has Pema been at the school?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What does 'I hate that I didn't' show about Dhruv's feelings?
qa.a: He felt ashamed that he let the group's quiet refusal stand, even though he likes Pema.

qa.q: What small step could Dhruv try on Monday?
qa.a: He could sit with Pema for one lunch, or bring one friend along, to show that group lines can be crossed.

qa.q: What is lunchtime likely like for Pema right now?
qa.a: Probably lonely, eating alone while the groups around him have already formed.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager running into his group's unspoken rule about who belongs and weighing whether to cross it.

passage: Tushar had exactly eight hundred rupees, saved from Diwali money and pocket money, and the white sneakers the senior boys wore cost three thousand. Sports day was Saturday; everyone would turn up in their best. At the market on Wednesday he found a copy pair for seven hundred, with a logo that was almost right. He held them longer than he meant to. His sister Parul, seventeen, watched him. 'You don't even like white shoes. You said they get dirty.' 'That's not the point.' 'Then what is?' He didn't answer. On the bus home he imagined walking past the seniors' bench and one of them nodding at him. Then he imagined the fake logo peeling off in the first race. He bought new laces for his old shoes instead, bright orange.

qa.q: How much money had Tushar saved?
qa.a: Eight hundred rupees.

qa.q: What did Tushar really want when he imagined a senior nodding at him?
qa.a: He wanted to be noticed and accepted by the older boys, more than he actually wanted the shoes.

qa.q: What could Parul say next that would help without shaming him?
qa.a: She could ask what he really wants from the seniors and point out things he already does that people respect.

qa.q: How does Parul see his wish for the shoes?
qa.a: She sees it is not about liking the shoes, since he said white ones get dirty, and she gently questions it.

grounding: Shows a teenager tempted to buy a trend item mainly to raise his standing with older boys, with little money to do it.

passage: In the corridor of the coaching centre in Lucknow, Hemant's group talked about one thing this month: an underground rap scene from Mumbai. Tushar, sixteen, had never heard of it on Monday. By Wednesday he was wearing his cap backwards and quoting lines he'd looked up at midnight. 'Which track's your favourite?' Hemant asked him at the tea stall. Tushar named the only one he remembered. Hemant grinned. 'That's everyone's first one. What else?' Tushar's mind went blank. He laughed too loudly and changed the subject to cricket. Walking home, he pulled the cap off and stuffed it in his bag. At home he played his father's old ghazal recordings, the music he actually hummed, and felt oddly relieved.

qa.q: Where did Hemant ask Tushar about his favourite track?
qa.a: At the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did Tushar laugh too loudly and change the subject?
qa.a: He was embarrassed that his put-on interest had been exposed and wanted to escape the moment.

qa.q: What could Tushar try instead of faking interest?
qa.a: He could ask Hemant to show him a few tracks honestly, or share the ghazals he really likes.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Tushar's sudden interest?
qa.a: He may have guessed it was new or put on, though his grin suggests he was not being cruel.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager adopting a trend to rise in a popular group's eyes and feeling the strain of it.

passage: The whole gang in Samir's colony in Hyderabad got the same buzz cut the week before term started. 'Your turn tomorrow,' they told him at the gate. Samir, fifteen, had been growing his curls since summer; he liked tying them back when he played the tabla. That night he stood in front of the mirror, pulling the curls straight, trying to picture himself without them. His neighbour Kashish, sixteen, out walking her dog, saw him on the steps later. 'You look like someone going to a punishment.' 'They're all doing it.' 'Do you want to?' He took a long time to answer. 'I want them to stop calling me the different one.' Next morning he went to the barber, asked for just a trim, and walked to the gate with his heart thumping.

qa.q: What instrument does Samir play?
qa.a: He plays the tabla.

qa.q: What did Samir's answer to Kashish show about what he wanted?
qa.a: He didn't want the haircut itself; he wanted to stop being singled out, so he felt torn between belonging and staying himself.

qa.q: What could help Samir if the group teases him about the trim?
qa.a: He could answer lightly and confidently, and spend time with people like Kashish who accept him as he is.

qa.q: What would change if Samir's friends had treated the haircut as optional?
qa.a: He could keep his curls without feeling he was risking his place in the group.

grounding: Shows a teenager torn between keeping his own look and matching his friends, and choosing his own way.

passage:
'Rajni, the group decided. Black dresses, all nine of us, for the farewell photo.'
'I heard.' Rajni kept folding Nani's green saree on the bed.
Mumma, from the doorway: 'That's the one you wanted to wear, na?'
'Wanted.'
Vandana sat down beside her. 'You'll look like the odd one out in the photo.'
'I know.'
'So?'
'So I've been thinking about it for three days.' Rajni ran her thumb along the border. 'Nani wore this to her own farewell. I wanted to wear it to mine.'
Mumma said nothing, which Rajni knew was deliberate.
Vandana sighed. 'What if you wear it for the function and change for the group photo?'
'That's... not bad.' Rajni looked up. 'Or I wear it the whole time and stand in the middle.'
Vandana laughed. 'Okay, bold. I'll stand next to you.'

qa.q: Who wore the green saree to her own farewell?
qa.a: Nani wore it to her own farewell.

qa.q: What does Rajni running her thumb along the border suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels torn, deeply attached to the saree and to Nani yet pulled by the wish to fit in with the group.

qa.q: How did Mumma support Rajni in this scene?
qa.a: She reminded her of what she had wanted and then stayed quiet, leaving the decision to Rajni.

qa.q: How does Vandana's view change during the talk?
qa.a: She starts by warning Rajni she will stand out, then offers a compromise and finally chooses to stand beside her.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager weighing her own wish against her group's plan to match, with her friend and mother present.

passage: 'Reena, you slammed your laptop shut when your coach said your essay was weak,' said Dhruv Mama. 'I did worse at your age. I was sixteen and editor of the school magazine. A teacher returned my article covered in red, and I told her, in front of everyone, that she didn't understand humour. Then I went home and sulked. My father read the red marks and said, "Half of these are right. Which half?" So I sat and sorted them. Seven were fair. Three I still disagreed with. Next day I thanked her for the seven and asked, politely, if we could discuss the three. She agreed with me on two. We ran that magazine together for two more years.'

qa.q: How many of the teacher's comments did young Dhruv decide were fair?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What did young Dhruv feel when the article came back covered in red?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defensive, which is why he snapped at the teacher and sulked at home.

qa.q: What could Reena try with her coach's comments?
qa.a: She could sort them into fair and unclear ones, thank the coach for the fair ones and ask calmly about the rest.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Dhruv came back politely?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and more willing to listen, since she agreed with him on two points.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from defensiveness to sorting criticism fairly and resolving the disagreement politely.

passage: Twenty minutes before their group presented, Sonali scrolled through Chaitanya's slides in the school computer room and frowned. 'Too much text. Nobody will read this.' Chaitanya, sixteen, felt heat rise up his neck; he had stayed up till one making them. He opened his mouth, closed it, and breathed out. 'Show me which ones.' She pointed at four. Meanwhile the fourth member, who had only done the survey, muttered that it was all fine. Chaitanya didn't snap at him either. 'You know the survey numbers best. Can you explain slide six out loud instead of us reading it?' The boy nodded, surprised. With eight minutes left they cut the text to headings. Then the printer jammed, so they presented straight from the screen. It went fine.

qa.q: How long before the presentation did Sonali look at the slides?
qa.a: Twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What does the heat rising up Chaitanya's neck suggest he felt, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: He felt stung after working late, but he paused and breathed so he could listen instead of snapping.

qa.q: Which choice helped the group most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sonali to show which slides were weak, because it turned criticism into specific fixes under time pressure.

qa.q: How might the quiet fourth member have felt when Chaitanya gave him slide six?
qa.a: Surprised and included, since he was given a real part instead of blame. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teenager taking blunt feedback calmly and smoothing group tension under time pressure.

passage: On the bus home through São Paulo traffic, Priscila, sixteen, watched the brown haze sit over the towers and felt the familiar tightness start. Geography class had been about rising seas again. She did the maths in her head: in thirty years she'd be forty-six. Would there be jobs? Would the coast still be there? What was the point of studying for exams about a world that might be falling apart? At home she lay on the floor with her earphones in and no music playing. Her brother Felix, twelve, stepped over her. 'You're doing the floor thing again.' 'Everything's broken, Felix.' He considered this, then lay down beside her. 'Is dinner broken? Mãe made feijoada.' She laughed despite herself and sat up.

qa.q: What had geography class been about?
qa.a: Rising seas.

qa.q: What does Priscila lying on the floor with no music playing suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt weighed down and withdrawn, overwhelmed by worry about the future.

qa.q: How could a parent or teacher support Priscila with these feelings?
qa.a: They could listen without dismissing her worries, help her find one small real action, and involve a counsellor if the dread keeps growing.

qa.q: How does Felix seem to see his sister's 'floor thing'?
qa.a: He is used to it and doesn't argue; he joins her and uses humour to pull her back to something ordinary.

grounding: Shows a teenager's diffuse dread about the world's future and her place in it, eased a little by her brother.

passage: The school library was meant to be silent, but Seema kept clicking her pen. 'Did you see the pictures from the floods up north? And fees going up again, and my brother still without a job after his degree.' Himani, beside her, closed her book. 'You've been like this all week.' 'Because it's all the same thing. Adults broke everything and we're supposed to fix it by writing essays about the monsoon.' Her voice rose; the librarian looked over. Seema pressed her forehead to the cool table. 'I'm not even sad. I'm just angry at nothing and everything.' Himani slid a note across: 'Walk after this period? The counsellor's door is open on Thursdays too.' Seema read it twice and nodded without lifting her head.

qa.q: What was Seema clicking in the library?
qa.a: Her pen.

qa.q: What did Seema mean by 'angry at nothing and everything'?
qa.a: She feels a broad, heavy frustration about the world and her future that does not point at one clear thing.

qa.q: What makes Himani's note a helpful response?
qa.a: It offers a simple next step and mentions the counsellor without lecturing or embarrassing Seema in the library.

qa.q: How might the librarian have seen Seema's raised voice?
qa.a: She may have seen only a noisy student, without knowing the worry underneath.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's general frustration and dread about the world, and a friend responding with care.

passage: Last monsoon I found my grandfather's old valve radio in the storeroom, dead and covered in dust. I don't know why it grabbed me, but it did. For months I skipped cricket, spent my pocket money on second-hand parts from the electronics lane, and watched repair videos till my eyes burned. My friend Zainab said, "Nitin, you talk about capacitors the way other people talk about cricket scores." When the radio finally crackled into an old Hindi song one night in January, I actually cried a little. Looking back, it wasn't really about the radio. It was the feeling of caring about something so much that time disappeared. My marks dipped that term, and I had to fix that too. But now I repair radios for three neighbours, and I want to study electronics.

qa.q: Where did Nitin find the old radio?
qa.a: In the storeroom.

qa.q: Why did Nitin cry a little when the radio played?
qa.a: Months of intense effort had finally worked, and the moment meant a lot to Nitin.

qa.q: What could Nitin do to keep this passion without the marks dipping again?
qa.a: Nitin could set fixed repair hours around study time, perhaps with a parent or teacher helping to plan them.

qa.q: How does Zainab seem to see Nitin's passion?
qa.a: Zainab teases Nitin about it, but clearly noticed how deeply Nitin cared.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense emotional investment in a hobby that grows into a direction for study.

passage: Teacher's note, eco-club, October. Disha has changed since the neem tree near the back gate was marked for cutting to widen the parking. She has come to every club meeting early, with printouts about the birds that nest in it and a petition signed by 212 students. She drew the tree's canopy on chart paper and worked out how much of the Class 1 line it shades at noon. When Rajni suggested they plant saplings elsewhere instead, Disha's voice shook: 'Saplings won't shade anyone for twenty years.' She apologised later for snapping. Next step: I have arranged for Disha and Rajni to present both ideas together to the principal on Monday, and reminded Disha to get some sleep; she looks tired.

qa.q: How many students signed the petition?
qa.a: 212 students.

qa.q: Why did Disha's voice shake when Rajni suggested saplings?
qa.a: She cared intensely about saving the tree and felt the saplings idea missed what mattered to her.

qa.q: Why is presenting both ideas together a wise step?
qa.a: It channels Disha's energy into a fair proposal and protects her friendship with Rajni, while the teacher also watches her tiredness. 👍

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when Disha snapped?
qa.a: Probably hurt or taken aback, since she was trying to help, though Disha's apology may have eased it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's intense drive for a cause, seen and gently guided by a teacher.

passage: The selection list went up on the notice board at 3:55, five minutes before the last bus. Sarika's name wasn't on it. She read it once, shrugged, and said loudly, 'Basketball is boring anyway.' Sunaina, who had been picked, stared at her. There was no time to talk; they ran for the bus, which was packed and roaring with Class 8 boys singing. Squeezed against the door, Sunaina tried: 'You practised every morning for two months.' 'So? Whatever. Doesn't matter.' Sarika put both earphones in and turned to the window. But Sunaina saw her grip the rail so hard her knuckles went pale. At her stop, Sarika got down without saying bye. That night Sunaina texted: 'Not going to pretend it doesn't matter. Call me whenever.'

qa.q: What time did the selection list go up?
What does Sarika gripping the rail suggest, despite her words?
qa.a: It suggests she was hurt and upset, hiding it behind a show of not caring.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do next that respects Sarika's need to protect herself?
qa.a: She could give her space tonight and check in privately later, without forcing her to admit she is hurt. 🤍

qa.q: What might it be like for Sunaina, being picked while her friend wasn't?
qa.a: She may feel happy but guilty, and worried about losing her friend over it.

grounding: Shows a teenager using a show of not caring to shield herself from the pain of rejection, on a crowded rushed journey.

passage: On results morning, the flat in Chennai was too quiet. Amma had lit the lamp twice. Appa kept refreshing the school website on his phone. Harsha, seventeen, sat on the sofa eating cereal slowly. 'Aren't you checking?' asked his brother Kishore, thirteen. 'Why? It's just marks. They don't define anything.' He said it the way he had said it all week, flat and bored. Kishore noticed the cereal had gone soggy and Harsha hadn't taken a bite for ten minutes. When Appa said, 'It's up,' Harsha didn't move. Kishore sat down beside him, close. 'I'll read it first if you want.' Harsha's jaw worked. 'Yeah. Okay. You read it.'

qa.q: How many times had Amma lit the lamp?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why was Harsha acting bored about the results?
qa.a: He likely cared a lot and was afraid of being disappointed, so acting detached protected him.

qa.q: What did Kishore get right in how he helped?
qa.a: He didn't argue with Harsha's act; he sat close and offered to read the result first, which let Harsha accept support.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa read Harsha's flat mood?
qa.a: They might think he truly doesn't care, or see through it, since their own nervousness is obvious.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager feigning indifference to shield himself from a feared disappointment, noticed by his younger brother.
